V02-J-001: Schools sort children by year of birth so routinely that the practice seems like a law of nature rather than an administrative convenience. Yet grouping by age assumes that children born within the same twelve months are ready for the same material at the same moment, an assumption that every experienced teacher knows to be false. In classrooms that deliberately mix ages, the older children consolidate what they know by explaining it, and the younger ones see, in the work of those just ahead of them, what the next step looks like. None of this makes mixed-age teaching easy: it demands careful planning and a teacher able to manage several levels at once, and without these it can fail badly. But that difficulty is a reason to prepare teachers for the task, not a reason to treat the age-graded class as the only sensible arrangement.
V02-J-002: Comparisons of test scores taken at the end of one school year and the start of the next have often suggested that children lose ground over the long holiday, and that children from poorer homes lose more. The finding has been used to argue that much of the gap between richer and poorer pupils opens not in school but outside it. Later work has complicated the picture. Some of the apparent loss depends on which tests are used and how their scores are scaled, and some estimates shrink considerably when the same children are measured in a different way. What survives scrutiny is more modest: holiday loss is real for some children, but it is smaller and less consistent than first reported, so it cannot by itself account for the gap, even if the long break remains a time when unequal home resources count for more than usual.
V02-J-003: A familiar remedy for textbooks that students find hard is to rewrite them in shorter sentences with commoner words, guided by formulas that score a text by the length of its words and sentences. The formulas do measure something, but what makes a passage hard to understand is often not its vocabulary so much as the gaps it leaves for the reader to fill. Cutting one long sentence into three short ones frequently removes the very words, such as because, although and therefore, that told the reader how the ideas were related; the result scores as easier and is harder to follow. None of this means that dense prose is a virtue or that difficult words never obstruct learning. It means that a readability score measures surface features, and a text revised to improve its score can lose the connective tissue on which comprehension depends.
V02-J-004: It is widely believed that a teacher's expectations can shape how well pupils perform: tell a teacher that certain children are about to blossom, and they will. There is evidence that expectations matter, since teachers who expect more of a pupil may give that pupil more attention, more time to answer questions and more demanding work. But the effects found in careful studies are usually modest, and they tend to be larger for younger children and for pupils whom the teacher does not yet know well. Expectations, in other words, are one influence among many, not a force that can by itself transform a child's results.
V02-J-005: It seems obvious that an operation cannot work by suggestion: the knife either repairs the tissue or it does not. For this reason, many surgical procedures entered routine use on the strength of surgeons' observations that their patients felt better afterwards. But patients who undergo surgery also receive attention, hope and a period of rest, and their symptoms often fluctuate and improve on their own. When some procedures have been tested against sham operations, in which patients are anaesthetised and given an incision but the key step is omitted, the improvement in the two groups has turned out to be similar. Such trials raise real ethical questions, since the sham group bears risk without the prospect of direct benefit. Yet without them, it is hard to know whether an operation helps because of what the surgeon does or because of everything that surrounds it.
V02-J-006: Much of what is believed about diet and health rests on asking people what they eat. The objection usually raised against such surveys is that people forget, and forgetting, being random, merely adds noise. The deeper difficulty is that the errors are not random. People tend to under-report foods they regard as unhealthy and over-report those they think virtuous, and the size of the distortion varies with body weight, with education and with how much a person cares about appearing healthy. Since those same characteristics are themselves linked to health, the error can manufacture associations or hide real ones, rather than simply blurring them. This does not make dietary surveys useless; for some questions they are the only practical source. But it means that a large sample, which cures random error, offers no protection against this kind.
V02-J-007: Studies that follow people over many years have found that those who report feeling lonely or socially isolated tend to die earlier than those who do not, and the association has led some to describe loneliness as a threat to public health. The finding is consistent and worth taking seriously. It is not, however, a simple demonstration that loneliness causes illness. People who are already unwell may withdraw from others, and poverty or disability can produce both isolation and poor health. Researchers try to adjust for such factors, but the most that can be said with confidence is that loneliness and early death travel together, and that loneliness may contribute to it.
V02-J-008: Hospitals that check whether staff clean their hands by sending observers onto the wards routinely record high rates of compliance. The rates are less impressive than they look. Staff who notice an observer wash more often while the observer is present, so the audit measures behaviour under observation, which is precisely the condition that does not hold for most of a working day. Where observed rates have been compared with counts from electronic dispensers or with unannounced checks, the observed rates have often turned out considerably higher. The point is not that staff are dishonest, nor that audits are pointless, since being watched does improve hand hygiene for a time. It is that a measure which changes the behaviour it measures cannot tell us how people behave when no one is looking.
V02-J-009: Two ideas of the residential street compete in suburban planning. The grid connects every street to several others, so drivers and walkers can take many routes and no single road carries the whole load. The cul-de-sac layout, with its looping roads and dead ends, keeps through traffic out, and residents of the closed streets often value the quiet and the safety of children playing outside. The difficulty is that the quiet is bought with distance: a shop a few hundred metres away as the crow flies may be more than a kilometre away by road, so residents drive for trips they might have walked, and the few roads that connect the loops carry heavy traffic. Each layout serves something real; the cul-de-sac simply moves its costs out of sight of those who enjoy its benefits.
V02-J-010: When rain falls on a field or a forest, much of the water soaks into the soil, and what runs off reaches the streams slowly. When the same rain falls on roofs, roads and car parks, almost none of it soaks in; it is gathered by gutters and drains and delivered to the river within minutes. A city can therefore flood after a storm that would have caused no trouble before the land was built on, not because more rain falls but because the rain reaches the river all at once. Wider drains can carry more water away, but they also speed its journey, which is why some cities now try to slow runoff with green roofs, permeable paving and ponds.
V02-J-011: In places where many people cycle, the risk of injury for each cyclist tends to be lower than in places where few do. This pattern is often read as proof that drivers become more careful when cyclists are common, so that simply encouraging more cycling will make it safer. The pattern is real, but the causal story may run partly the other way. Cities that have built protected lanes and calmed their traffic attract more cyclists precisely because cycling there is already safer, and more cautious people take up cycling only when it feels safe. Driver adaptation may contribute as well; nobody needs to deny it. What the pattern does not support is the hope that numbers alone, without the infrastructure that draws them, will deliver safety.
V02-J-012: Faster roads and railways are usually justified by the time they will save commuters. Yet in many cities and over long periods, the average time people spend travelling to work each day has stayed surprisingly stable. The explanation is that people treat travel time, not distance, as the quantity to be budgeted. When a new motorway cuts the journey, many households eventually move further out, to larger and cheaper homes, until the commute is roughly as long as it was before. The investment is not wasted: people gain space and a wider choice of jobs and housing. But its benefit arrives as a larger city rather than as the shorter commute that was promised.
V02-J-013: Most people feel that they would be obliged to help a stranger in danger in front of them, yet feel no comparable obligation to help a stranger in equal danger on another continent. Some philosophers conclude that this feeling is simply a bias: distance, they argue, cannot by itself make a moral difference, so our duties to the distant are as strong as our duties to the near. The argument is powerful, but it moves too quickly. Distance usually travels with other features that may matter, such as whether one is uniquely placed to help, whether one's help will actually arrive, and whether many others could help equally well. To show that the feeling is mere bias, one must show that it survives when these features are held constant, and that is harder than the argument assumes.
V02-J-014: When a crime is discovered decades after it was committed, it is sometimes said that punishing the offender now punishes a different person: the frail old man in the dock shares a name with the young man who did the deed, but little else. The objection has force where punishment is meant to reform, for a person who has long since changed has nothing left to reform. It has less force where punishment is meant to answer the wrong itself, to affirm that the victim mattered and that the act was not acceptable. For that purpose what matters is not whether the offender has changed but whether he is the one responsible, and a change of character, however real, does not transfer responsibility to someone else. Time may therefore weaken some reasons for punishment while leaving others intact.
V02-J-015: Many people believe there is a moral difference between telling a lie and saying something true that is designed to mislead. Asked whether he has been drinking, the driver who answers 'I had a glass of water an hour ago' has not lied, though he hopes the listener will draw a false conclusion. One defence of the distinction is that the misleader leaves the listener a share of the responsibility, since the false belief comes from the listener's own inference. But the listener drew that inference precisely because the speaker counted on it. Whatever difference remains seems to lie less in the harm done to the listener than in what the speaker permits himself: a rule against outright falsehood that he keeps even while evading its purpose.
V02-J-016: Arranging choices so that people are steered towards better outcomes, by setting a sensible default for pension saving or putting fruit at eye level in a canteen, is often defended on the ground that no option is forbidden and anyone can choose otherwise. Critics reply that such arrangements are manipulative, working on inertia and habit rather than on reason. The reply is weaker than it sounds, because some arrangement is unavoidable: a canteen must put something at eye level, and a pension scheme must have some default. The real question is therefore not whether choices will be shaped but by whom and for whose benefit, and whether the shaping is open enough that people could object to it if they knew of it.
V02-J-017: A specialist asked to introduce a field to newcomers frequently leaves them more confused than before, and ill will rarely has anything to do with it. Understanding, once gained, erases the memory of what it was like to lack it. So the specialist jumps over steps that now feel self-evident, reaches for terms that have become automatic and misjudges how much time a novice needs to keep up. The mastery that earns someone the right to teach thus hides from that person the view of the subject a newcomer has. The best teachers get round this not by knowing less but by repeatedly testing what their audience has in fact understood.
V02-J-018: In a familiar kind of experiment, people given a simple object such as a mug ask for considerably more to part with it than others, not given one, will pay to acquire it. The gap has been taken as evidence that owning a thing makes us value it more, simply because it is ours. The finding has proved robust in many settings, but its size depends on circumstances. It tends to shrink among experienced traders, who regard goods as stock to be sold, and it is larger for items people expect to keep and use than for those they hold only for exchange. Ownership, it seems, raises value most when a thing is seen as part of one's possessions rather than as a token in a market.
V02-J-019: People tend to overestimate how many others share their opinions, habits and preferences. Part of the reason is that we spend most of our time with people like ourselves, so the sample of views we meet is not representative of the wider population. Part is that our own choices seem to us the natural response to a situation, so we assume that others facing it would choose the same. The tendency is not simply vanity; it arises from the limited and familiar evidence that each of us has about what other people think. It also helps explain why people are often surprised when an election or a survey reveals how divided opinion really is.
V02-J-020: Ask people how well they understand how a zip, a flush toilet or a bicycle works, and most will rate their understanding highly. Ask them then to explain, step by step, how the device actually works, and many find they cannot; when asked to rate their understanding again, they mark it down. The confidence was not a lie but a confusion: familiarity with using something, and knowing that an explanation exists somewhere, feels from the inside like possessing the explanation. Notably, the gap is narrower for facts and procedures, such as the names of capital cities or how to tie a knot, where people can check their knowledge by trying to recall or perform it.
V02-J-021: For years it was widely accepted that self-control draws on a limited resource, so that resisting one temptation leaves a person less able to resist the next. The idea was supported by many small experiments and fitted the everyday experience of feeling worn out after a demanding day. When the effect was retested in large studies run to a common plan across many laboratories, it proved much smaller than the earlier work had suggested, and in some cases indistinguishable from zero. It would be too quick to conclude that people never tire of exercising self-control. What the episode shows is that a stack of small studies, each published because it found an effect, can make a weak or absent phenomenon look established, and that agreement with everyday experience is no substitute for a test designed in advance.
V02-J-022: Languages that oblige speakers to choose between a familiar and a respectful form of 'you' are sometimes thought more hierarchical than those, like modern English, that use a single form for everyone. The comparison is misleading. Speakers of English mark distance and rank in other ways: through first names or titles, through how directly they make requests, through who may start a conversation and who may end it. A language without the grammatical choice has not abolished the social one; it has moved it elsewhere, often to places where it is harder for a newcomer to notice. If anything, the explicit pronoun makes the rules of respect easier to see and therefore easier to learn.
V02-J-023: Gossip has a poor reputation: it is condemned as idle, malicious and a waste of time. A more sympathetic view, now common among those who study small communities, holds that gossip performs a social function, spreading knowledge of who can be trusted and deterring cheats who fear for their reputations. This view is a useful corrective, but it can slide into a defence of gossip as such. The same mechanism that deters the cheat also punishes the nonconformist, the newcomer and anyone whose private life departs from local expectation, and it does so without a hearing. To say that gossip enforces norms is to say nothing yet about whether the norms deserve enforcing, or whether those it targets had any chance to answer.
V02-J-024: Children in families that eat together regularly tend, on average, to do better at school and to report fewer emotional difficulties. This has led to the advice that parents should make shared meals a priority. Yet families that manage regular meals together often differ in other ways too: they may have more predictable working hours, more money and less conflict at home. Some of what looks like the effect of the meal may be the effect of the kind of household that can arrange one. The meal may still help, but the evidence for it is weaker than the advice suggests.
V02-J-025: Many traditional societies set out how long the bereaved should mourn, what they should wear and when they might return to ordinary life. Such rules are easily dismissed today as rigid impositions on private feeling. But they also did something for the grieving. They told others how to behave towards the bereaved, gave the mourner permission to withdraw for a time, and marked a point at which life could resume without guilt. Where the rules have faded, people are often left unsure how long grief is allowed to last and what their friends expect of them. The old customs had their costs, but they offered a shared structure that private feeling alone does not supply.
